content_metadata.description: A video analysis detailing the presence and significance of interstellar objects within our solar system, emphasizing ongoing discoveries and potential future research.

qAndA.answer: The video mentions a recent study suggesting there could be about 10 million interstellar objects in a halo surrounding our solar system.
qAndA.question: What is the estimated number of interstellar objects potentially surrounding our solar system?

qAndA.answer: The video explains that these objects provide clues about the chemical makeup and formation of other planetary systems, offering insights into the broader universe.
qAndA.question: What is the significance of studying interstellar objects?

qAndA.answer: The video states that the objects in the Oort cloud are small, cold, and very faint, making them challenging to detect even with advanced telescopes.
qAndA.question: Why is it difficult to detect most interstellar objects in the Oort cloud?

qAndA.answer: The video discusses Oumuamua, the first known interstellar object detected in our solar system, and Comet 2I/Borisov, another confirmed interstellar visitor.
qAndA.question: What specific examples of interstellar objects are mentioned in the video?

qAndA.answer: The video explains that scientists can differentiate them based on their unique orbital paths and motion, as interstellar interlopers exhibit distinct characteristics.
qAndA.question: How can astronomers distinguish between comets that originated in our solar system and those from interstellar space?

narrativeProgression.description: This scene introduces the concept of interstellar objects and how our solar system captures them temporarily, using Oumuamua as the first known example.
Oumuamua was the first interstellar object astronomers spotted in our solar system.

scenes.title: Oumuamua

videoEditingDetails.description: Text appears, overlayed on top of the moving rocks animation, outlining a recent study suggesting that our solar system may be surrounded by 10 million interstellar objects. The text describes Oumuamua.
Transition to a static background of the Milky Way Galaxy. Text explaining how our solar system captures interstellar objects, using Oumuamua as an example.

scenes.contextualRelevance: Explains the gravitational slingshot effect on interstellar objects.

narrativeProgression.description: The scene builds on the previous one by explaining the gravitational slingshot effect and how it applies to captured interstellar objects, highlighting their temporary residence in our solar system.

scenes.title: Gravitational Slingshot

videoEditingDetails.description: Text continues over the Milky Way background, explaining how captured interstellar objects are eventually flung back out into space by the Sun's gravity.

scenes.contextualRelevance: Discusses the Oort cloud and the future of detecting interstellar objects.

keyMoments.changeDescription: The mood shifts slightly towards pensiveness as the limitations of current technology are discussed.

narrativeProgression.description: This scene delves into the potential population of interstellar objects in the Oort cloud and their scientific value. It also introduces future telescopes and surveys that could aid in detecting these objects.

scenes.title: The Oort Cloud and Future Observations

videoEditingDetails.description: Text continues, suggesting that a significant portion of the Oort cloud may consist of captured interstellar objects. It also explains the challenges of detecting these objects and the need for advanced technology.
Transition to a static illustration showing Neptune's orbit, the Kuiper belt, and the Oort cloud. This visual helps viewers grasp the scale and location of the Oort cloud.

Transition back to the Milky Way background with text describing the scientific significance of studying interstellar objects and mentioning telescopes that can potentially contribute to future discoveries.

scenes.contextualRelevance: Explains how astronomers distinguish interstellar objects from solar system comets.

narrativeProgression.description: The scene concludes by exploring methods for differentiating between homegrown comets and interstellar interlopers, promising future advancements in understanding our solar system's origins.

scenes.title: Distinguishing Interstellar Objects

videoEditingDetails.description: The text discusses how astronomers differentiate between homegrown comets and interstellar interlopers based on their orbital paths and motion.
Transition to a dark background with gears rotating in the center. Text appears expressing gratitude for watching and inviting donations. The website of the channel is also displayed.

Our Suns orbit fairly often. OUMUA may not be as unusual as we thought. As our solar system makes its 230 million new orbit around the outer edges of the Milky Way galaxy.
It occasionally passes by bits of cosmic jetsome discarded by other stars, straight comets, asteroids.
And other chunks of space rock that got kicked out of their original homes, just like our solar system may once have booted out a whole planet.
Once in a while, these objects drift through our solar system, stirring our interest in some really wild speculation.
But our solar system may actually have a swarm of interstellar objects trapped in its outskirts.
According to a recent study by University of Edinburgh Gastronomer and statistician Jorge Penarabia, published in the journal monthly notices of the Royal Astronomical Society.
What's new? Weilding an amount of math that is truly terrifying to behold.
Penarabia modeled how gravity of our Sun and the gravity of the Milky Way galaxy affect interstellar objects that come near our solar system.
OUMUA was the first interstellar object astronomers ever spotted in our solar system, but it almost wasn't the first to arrive, and it won't be the last.

As a chunk of interstellar rock, like OUMUA Mua, orbits the center of our galaxy, it happens to pass close to a star system, where eight planets and a collection of smaller objects orbit a yellowish star.
The tidal pull of the Milky Way's gravity slows the stray asteroid just enough that the Sun's gravity can capture it and pull it in for a very brief orbital dance.
Our newly captured interstellar visitor hasn't settled into a permanent, stable orbit, though.
Instead, it will hold on for just a few laps, or maybe just part of a lap.
Before the Sun slings it back out into interstellar space with more energy than it had before the encounter.
It will end up on a higher, faster orbit around the center of the Milky Way.
In other words, this is exactly the same principle that we use to send ships to the outer solar system, Penarabia tells Inverse.
Cassini, new horizons, and the Voyager probes all used similar maneuvers to reach their far-flung destinations.
Essentially, the Milky Way's gravity slows the interstellar object down enough to fall into the Sun's orbit,
and the Sun is providing a gravitational slingshot. As it pulls the asteroid into its orbit, it causes the asteroid to speed up, until that speed becomes enough for the comet to escape again.
Because the Sun is constantly capturing new interstellar objects and kicking out old ones, we keep a pretty much constant number of them in a rocky halo around our solar system.
According to Penarabia, these briefly captured interstellar objects may make up a sizable chunk of the odd cloud.
The hypothetical cloud of icy objects surrounding the farthest outskirts of our solar system, and some of them end up on paths that occasionally bring them as far inward as Earth's orbit.
It's hard to say how many interstellar objects are part of our solar system at any given moment, however.
Astronomers aren't actually sure exactly how many comets and other objects are in the odd cloud, estimates, based on the tiny number of comets that get close enough to Earth for us to see.
Range from hundreds of billions to trillions, let alone how many of those objects are hand-me-downs from other solar systems, briefly snatched up from interstellar space.
Even if those objects are out there, we don't have the technology yet to detect them in big numbers, says Penarabia.
We only see very rare occurrences like Umuamua and Borussoff, based on the two or three interstellar objects astronomers have detected so far.
Penarabia says his model predicts there should be about ten million of them in the halo of straight space flots and surrounding our solar system.
And a few hundred of them may even be orbiting about as close to the sun as Neptune.

Here's the background. In late 2017, astronomers discovered an alien intruder in our solar system, along Nara Slabbov-Rock, somewhere between 101,000 meters long, moving on a course that suggested it was just passing through our solar system.

On its way from and to somewhere out in interstellar space, and in October 2019, comet 2i, Borussoff sipped through our inner solar system on a trajectory that suggested it had come from somewhere outside our comfy little stellar neighborhood.
Astronomers branded Borussoff, broke comet, and studied it intently.
These objects' presence reminds us that our solar system isn't in a hermetic bubble, isolated from the rest of the galaxy.
I think my work is probably telling us that there should be many more than people have thought, says Penarabia.
This illustration shows, roughly, where the odd cloud should be in relation to the more familiar central part of our solar system, and how far our cloud of space debris extends outward.
Why it matters? Objects like Vumuamu are in Borussoff are compelling to think about just because they're from elsewhere.
However, they're scientifically interesting because they bring us evidence about the chemical makeup of other planetary systems, as well as clues about how those systems formed and evolved.
And if Penarabia is right, then we have plenty of interstellar objects in our own solar system,
just waiting to be found and studied, if we can find them, that is.
If you can detect a sizable population of trapped objects, then we are going to have a lot of information about how many there are in the Milky Way floating around.
And what is the composition where they come in different solar systems, says Penarabia.
And if so, what kind of properties those solar systems had in the past, in their age distribution?
We'll be super interesting, but finding those objects is going to be a challenge.
Penarabia's model says they should be there, but most are too far out to see even with our most advanced telescopes, for now.
What's next? Even the James Webb Space Telescope can't reveal most of the odd cloud to us.
The small, cold objects out, there are just too faint even for JWST's powerful instruments to detect.
But JWST isn't our only chance to find and track the small objects that mostly dwell at the fringes of our solar system.
Astronomers often spot previously unknown comets in surveys like the Sloan Digital Sky Survey and the Catalina Sky Survey.
The ESA's Gire Observatory and the Vera Rubin Observatory will also help spot new to us comets, perhaps increasing our current list by several orders of magnitude.
And, according to Penarabia, we can tell homegrown comets from interstellar interlopers by their paths and their motion.
If we could measure the orbit of a large number of objects, which is going to happen in the next few years, then we should start to see this kind of distinct population.
Which is probably also distinct in composition, says Penarabia.
I wouldn't be surprised if objects that have been trapped from the interstellar environment have this different composition than objects that were formed in the solar system.
So there will be, potentially, many different ways to see whether we can differentiate them from the rest of the comets that form in the solar system.
